9701-1.3.1.motivate: Saying an atom's electrons sit "in shells" is too coarse to explain why potassium behaves as it does. Three nested words fix that: shell, sub-shell, orbital.
9701-1.3.1.establish: A **shell** is a group of orbitals with the same **principal quantum number** $n$ ($n=1,2,3,\dots$); a larger $n$ means further from the nucleus and higher in energy. A shell is divided into **sub-shells** (s, p, d), each being a group of orbitals of the same type and the same energy. An **orbital** is a region of space around the nucleus that holds a maximum of two electrons, with opposite spins. The **ground state** is the arrangement in which all the electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels.
9701-1.3.1.connect: With shell, sub-shell and orbital separated, the next step is counting: how many orbitals each sub-shell contains and therefore how many electrons it holds.
9701-1.3.1.note:
- Shell: orbitals with the same principal quantum number $n$; larger $n$ is further out and higher in energy.
- Sub-shell: orbitals of the same type (s, p, d) within a shell, all at the same energy.
- Orbital: a region of space holding at most 2 electrons, with opposite spins.
- Ground state: every electron in the lowest available energy level.
9701-1.3.1.self_explain: In your own words, why is "orbital" not just another word for "sub-shell"?

9701-1.3.2.motivate: If an orbital holds only two electrons, how can a p sub-shell hold six? The answer is simply how many orbitals each sub-shell is built from.
9701-1.3.2.establish: Each orbital holds a maximum of **2 electrons**. An **s sub-shell** is 1 orbital, so it holds 2 electrons. A **p sub-shell** is 3 orbitals, so it holds 6 electrons. A **d sub-shell** is 5 orbitals, so it holds 10 electrons. So sub-shell capacity $=2\times$ (number of orbitals). Shell capacities follow: $n=1$ holds 2 (1s), $n=2$ holds 8 (2s, 2p), $n=3$ holds 18 (3s, 3p, 3d). Note that there is no 1p and no 2d sub-shell.
9701-1.3.2.connect: Knowing each capacity, the only thing still missing before writing a configuration is the order in which the sub-shells are filled.
9701-1.3.2.note:
- Every orbital holds at most 2 electrons (opposite spins).
- s: 1 orbital, 2 electrons. p: 3 orbitals, 6 electrons. d: 5 orbitals, 10 electrons.
- Shell maxima: $n=1$ is 2, $n=2$ is 8, $n=3$ is 18.
- There is no 1p sub-shell and no 2d sub-shell.
9701-1.3.2.self_explain: A student writes $2p^6$ and calls 2p "an orbital holding six electrons". Which word is wrong, and what should it be?

9701-1.3.3.motivate: Potassium is $\ce{[Ar]}\,4s^1$, not $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^1$. Shell number alone does not decide which sub-shell fills next, so the energy order has to be learned.
9701-1.3.3.establish: In order of **increasing energy**: $1s<2s<2p<3s<3p<4s<3d<4p$. Within a shell, s is lower than p, which is lower than d. The one order that is not simply by $n$ is that **4s is lower in energy than 3d**, so 4s fills first: K is $\ce{[Ar]}\,4s^1$ and Ca is $\ce{[Ar]}\,4s^2$, and only at scandium does 3d begin to fill ($\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^1 4s^2$). Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels first, which is why this order is the filling order.
9701-1.3.3.connect: This order is the recipe followed in the next step, where electrons are placed one sub-shell at a time to build a full configuration.
9701-1.3.3.note:
- Increasing energy: $1s<2s<2p<3s<3p<4s<3d<4p$.
- Within a shell, s is below p, which is below d.
- 4s is below 3d in energy, so 4s fills before 3d (K, Ca fill 4s).
- Filling order and writing order differ: configurations are written with 3d before 4s.
9701-1.3.3.self_explain: Why does "$n=3$ is lower than $n=4$" not settle whether 3d or 4s fills first?

discover.stem: Which sub-shell receives the next electron after the 3p sub-shell of a calcium atom's argon core is full?

options.B: 4s, because 4s is lower in energy than 3d
options.C: 4p, because p follows s in each shell
options.D: 3f, because the third shell is not yet complete

discover.explanation: The 4s sub-shell lies lower in energy than 3d, so it fills first: Ca is $\ce{[Ar]}\,4s^2$. Electrons fill the lowest available energy level, which is not always the lowest $n$. There is no 3f sub-shell, and 4p is above 3d.

9701-1.3.4.motivate: An examiner asks for the electronic configuration of phosphorus, and wants every shell, sub-shell and orbital accounted for. One systematic routine does it every time.
9701-1.3.4.establish: Count the electrons, then fill sub-shells in energy order up to their capacities, writing each as (shell number)(letter)$^{\text{number of electrons}}$. Phosphorus (15 electrons) gives $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$: $2+2+6+2+3=15$. Within a sub-shell, electrons occupy separate orbitals before pairing, so the three 3p electrons give **3 unpaired electrons**, and sulfur's $3p^4$ gives 2. Always check that the superscripts add up to the electron count and that no sub-shell exceeds its capacity (s 2, p 6, d 10).
9701-1.3.4.connect: Filling single orbitals before pairing is a rule used here but not yet justified; the reason is inter-electron repulsion, which comes next.
9701-1.3.4.note:
- Count electrons, fill in energy order, write as $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 \dots$ with superscripts for electron numbers.
- Phosphorus (15 electrons) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3$, with 3 unpaired electrons.
- Within a sub-shell, fill orbitals singly before pairing: $3p^3$ gives 3 unpaired, $3p^4$ gives 2.
- Check: superscripts sum to the electron count, and no sub-shell is over capacity.
9701-1.3.4.self_explain: How would you check a written configuration for silicon is right without looking up the answer?

9701-1.3.5.motivate: Why should nature bother spreading three electrons over three separate 3p orbitals when they could crowd into one? Because electrons repel.
9701-1.3.5.establish: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, but they also repel each other. **Inter-electron repulsion** means two electrons sharing one orbital repel more strongly than two in separate orbitals of the same energy, so the orbitals of a sub-shell are filled **singly first, with parallel spins**, and pair up only once every orbital holds one electron (**Hund's rule**). This arrangement has the lowest energy. The same repulsion between a pair in one orbital (spin-pair repulsion) is why sulfur, with a paired 3p orbital, has a lower first ionisation energy than phosphorus.
9701-1.3.5.connect: This explanation is what makes a deduced configuration defensible, which matters as soon as ions and boxes are drawn.
9701-1.3.5.note:
- Electrons fill the lowest available energy levels, but they also repel one another.
- Hund's rule: orbitals of equal energy fill singly, with parallel spins, before any pairing.
- Two electrons in one orbital repel more than two in separate orbitals of the same energy.
- Spin-pair repulsion in a paired 3p orbital lowers the first ionisation energy of S below that of P.
9701-1.3.5.self_explain: Explain, in terms of repulsion, why a nitrogen atom has 3 unpaired electrons rather than 1.

9701-1.3.6.motivate: Iron forms both $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$. Deducing the configuration of an ion needs one extra decision: which electrons leave.
9701-1.3.6.establish: Work from the atom. For a given proton number, fill in energy order, then adjust for the charge: a positive charge means that many **fewer** electrons, a negative charge that many more. Electrons are **removed from the outermost occupied shell first**, so 4s electrons go before any 3d electron. Fe (26 electrons) is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^6 4s^2$, i.e. $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^6 4s^2$ in **shorthand** form; $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ is $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^6$ and $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ is $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^5$. Either the full or the shorthand convention is accepted.
9701-1.3.6.connect: A configuration such as $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^5$ is the starting point for drawing the same ion as boxes and arrows.
9701-1.3.6.note:
- Deduce the atom first, then add or remove electrons for the charge (positive means fewer).
- Remove electrons from the outermost shell first: 4s before 3d.
- Fe is $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^6 4s^2$, so $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ is $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^6$ and $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$ is $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^5$.
- Full ($1s^2 2s^2 \dots$) and shorthand ($\ce{[Ar]}\,\dots$) conventions are both acceptable.
9701-1.3.6.self_explain: Why is $\ce{Fe^{2+}}$ not $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^4 4s^2$, even though 4s fills before 3d?

discover.stem: An iron atom is $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^6 4s^2$. Which is the electronic configuration of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$?
discover.explanation: Three electrons are lost, taken from the outermost shell first: both 4s electrons, then one 3d electron, leaving $\ce{[Ar]}\,3d^5$. Option B removes them from 3d instead, C is the atom unchanged, and D adds electrons rather than removing them.

9701-1.3.7.motivate: A written $3d^6$ hides something a question may ask for: how many of those electrons are unpaired. Boxes and arrows show it at a glance.
9701-1.3.7.establish: In **electrons-in-boxes** notation each box is one orbital and each arrow is one electron, drawn up or down for the two opposite spins. A box with two opposite arrows holds a **pair**; a box with one arrow holds an **unpaired** electron. Draw the boxes of a sub-shell side by side (1 for s, 3 for p, 5 for d), label them, and fill by Hund's rule: one arrow in each box first, all parallel, then pair up. For Fe, $\ce{[Ar]}$ plus five 3d boxes holding 6 electrons (one pair and four single arrows, so 4 unpaired) and a full 4s box.
9701-1.3.7.connect: Boxes make the unpaired electrons visible, which is exactly what defines a free radical later in the chapter.
9701-1.3.7.note:
- One box is one orbital; one arrow is one electron, up or down for opposite spins.
- Two opposite arrows in a box are a pair; a single arrow is an unpaired electron.
- Boxes per sub-shell: s 1, p 3, d 5; fill singly with parallel arrows before pairing.
- Fe is $\ce{[Ar]}$ with $3d^6$ (one pair, 4 unpaired) and a full 4s box.
9701-1.3.7.self_explain: How many arrows, and how many of them unpaired, would you draw for the 3d boxes of $\ce{Fe^{3+}}$?

9701-1.3.8.motivate: An orbital is a region of space, so it has a shape. Papers ask you to sketch two of them, and to say which electrons sit in a sphere.
9701-1.3.8.establish: An **s orbital is spherical**, centred on the nucleus, and the sphere is larger for a larger principal quantum number (2s is bigger than 1s). A **p orbital is dumb-bell shaped**: two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus. There are three p orbitals in a p sub-shell, pointing along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes at $90^\circ$ to one another. Sketches should show the nucleus, the sphere or the two lobes, and for p orbitals the axis they lie along. In a ground-state carbon atom the orbital of lowest energy, 1s, is spherical.
9701-1.3.8.connect: Shapes complete the picture of an orbital as a region of space, the idea that bonding later builds on when orbitals overlap.
9701-1.3.8.note:
- s orbital: spherical and centred on the nucleus, larger for larger $n$.
- p orbital: dumb-bell shaped, two lobes either side of the nucleus.
- The three p orbitals lie along the $x$, $y$ and $z$ axes, at $90^\circ$ to each other.
- A sketch should show the nucleus and, for p, the axis the lobes lie along.
9701-1.3.8.self_explain: Which occupied orbital of a ground-state carbon atom is spherical, and which is not?

9701-1.3.9.motivate: Chlorine atoms attack alkanes while chloride ions do not. The reactive species has a name that comes straight from its electron arrangement.
9701-1.3.9.establish: A **free radical** is a species with **one or more unpaired electrons**. Nothing else is required: charge is irrelevant, so neutral atoms and molecules, cations and anions can all be radicals. $\ce{Cl}$ ($3s^2 3p^5$) and $\ce{O}$ have unpaired electrons and are radicals, as do $\ce{O^-}$ ($2p^5$) and $\ce{Cl^+}$ ($3p^4$). $\ce{Cl^-}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$ have every electron paired in full octets, so they are not radicals. Among molecules, $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NO2}$ each have an unpaired electron; $\ce{NH3}$ does not.
9701-1.3.9.connect: Unpaired electrons make radicals highly reactive, which is the basis of free-radical substitution in the halogenoalkanes chapters.
9701-1.3.9.note:
- A free radical is a species with one or more unpaired electrons.
- Charge does not matter: atoms, molecules, cations and anions can all be radicals.
- $\ce{Cl}$, $\ce{O^-}$ and $\ce{Cl^+}$ are radicals; $\ce{Cl^-}$ and $\ce{O^{2-}}$ are not.
- $\ce{NO}$ and $\ce{NO2}$ contain an unpaired electron; $\ce{NH3}$ does not.
9701-1.3.9.self_explain: Decide whether $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ is a free radical, and say what you had to work out to decide.
